title: Pakistan Asks US for $10 Billion Currency Backstop After Iran Mediation Role
excerpt: Islamabad has requested a rare exchange stabilization facility from the US Treasury, seeking to convert its diplomatic gains from the Iran war into economic leverage.
body:
Pakistan has asked the United States for a $10 billion exchange stabilization facility, according to a source briefed on the matter cited by Reuters — a request that, if approved, could fundamentally reshape the cash-strapped nation's economic trajectory.

In its pitch to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Islamabad is seeking a Bilateral Exchange Stabilization Support Facility worth $10 billion with a maturity of up to five years. The request is being reported for the first time and comes on the heels of Pakistan's role brokering diplomatic talks over the Iran war, which elevated its standing with the Trump administration.

Pakistan's finance ministry did not respond to Reuters' request for comment. The US Treasury declined to comment.

A Rare Financial Instrument

Exchange stabilization facilities are among the rarest backstops the US Treasury offers. Routed through the Exchange Stabilization Fund, they provide dollars, swaps, or guarantees to bolster foreign reserves and steady currencies. They are distinct from the permanent dollar swap lines the Federal Reserve maintains with major central banks.

https://x.com/arabnewspk/status/2079793589182189747

The precedent list is short. A 2025 package for Argentina was the first new foreign-government exchange stabilization facility since Uruguay in 2002, aside from Mexico's long-standing swap line — dating to the 1940s and now sized at $9 billion. Pakistan joining that list would mark a dramatic shift in US-Pakistan economic relations.

Why Pakistan Needs It Now

Pakistan narrowly avoided sovereign default in 2023, securing a $3 billion IMF standby arrangement before graduating to a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility and a separate $1.3 billion climate resilience loan. But its reserves remain precariously dependent on official financing, rollovers, and deposits from China and Saudi Arabia.

"A $10 billion American currency backstop would reduce Islamabad's dependence on Beijing and Riyadh — potentially reshuffling the regional balance of influence."

That vulnerability was laid bare in April when Pakistan repaid roughly $3.5 billion — one-fifth of its total reserves — to the United Arab Emirates. Saudi Arabia stepped in with $3 billion in fresh support, but the episode underscored how exposed Islamabad remains to shifts in bilateral goodwill.

The IMF programme, while stabilizing Pakistan's macroeconomic picture, has come at steep political cost: higher taxes, spending restraint, and limited room for development or welfare spending. Global ratings agency Fitch noted in April that adherence to the programme had supported Pakistan's funding capacity, but cautioned that rising energy costs and supply disruptions from the Middle East conflict could erode its foreign exchange buffers.

Pakistan's central bank projected in January that reserves could reach $20 billion by end of 2026, nearing their 2021 record. A US backstop would provide a powerful safety net toward that target.

Leveraging the Trump Connection

The exchange stabilization request is part of a broader Pakistani push to deepen economic ties with the Trump administration. That campaign has already produced several deals: a stablecoin agreement for cross-border payments with an affiliate of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's main crypto venture; a memorandum of understanding to redevelop the shuttered PIA-owned Roosevelt Hotel in New York; and courtship of US mining investment in Reko Diq, where the US Export-Import Bank has committed $1.2 billion in financing.

Foreign investment in Pakistan has remained thin, according to Reuters, deterred by recurring external crises, policy uncertainty, security risks, past profit-repatriation curbs, and a narrow export base. The country's credit rating sits deep in speculative-grade territory, keeping borrowing costs high.

Regional Implications for India

For India, Pakistan's bid to lock in a major US financial commitment carries strategic implications. A $10 billion American currency backstop would reduce Islamabad's dependence on Beijing and Riyadh — potentially reshuffling the regional balance of influence. It would also signal Washington's willingness to reward Pakistan's mediation role, a dynamic New Delhi will watch closely given its own positioning in the Iran conflict and broader US-India economic partnership.

"Treasury is committed to working with Congress to protect our nation's financial system, spur job growth, and strengthen the economy."

— Scott Bessent, US Treasury Secretary, in earlier Congressional testimony

India's diaspora, the world's largest source of remittances at nearly $138 billion annually, has long dwarfed Pakistan's overseas inflows. But any stabilization of the Pakistani rupee could affect cross-border transaction dynamics and competitive currency positioning in the region.

What Comes Next

The ball is now in Washington's court. US exchange stabilization decisions are made by the Treasury Secretary with broad discretion, though political considerations and Congressional scrutiny are inevitable for a commitment of this scale to Pakistan.

Key markers to watch: whether the IMF signals comfort with the arrangement alongside its existing $7 billion programme, how China and Saudi Arabia respond to a potential dilution of their financial leverage over Islamabad, and whether the facility — if approved — comes with conditions on governance, defence spending, or counterterrorism cooperation.

Pakistan's bet is that its Iran mediation has opened a window. Whether that window stays open long enough for a $10 billion commitment remains an open question.
